reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its primary purpose is to record and expose a purported technical-support scam call. The caller's Microsoft claim, request for an external-computer connection, and demand for 25 euros are presented as part of a testing interaction rather than as the video's own solicitation.

I just wanted to see whether you were genuine
You tried to you tried to scam me, so I'm wasting your time.
I'm calling you from windows operating systems on behalf of Microsoft Corporation
connection to external computer

opening.argument: The interaction links concrete viewer actions to a promised computer-protection outcome and a payment request. The caller directs the user to download and run Supremo, approve system changes, and connect to an external computer, then says registration is required to “protect your computer” and “fix your computer.” That is a direct action-to-benefit pathway, not merely discussion: the user must follow the remote-access process and pay the registration fee to obtain the promised repair and certificate. The pitch also makes the fee appear unusually attractive by contrasting 25 euros with an alleged 400-euro market cost.

we have to do the registration right now so that we can protect your computer we can fix your computer
registration fee, which is only 25 euros
it will cost you around 400 euros

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a test does not remove the solicitation actually presented. The recorded interaction contains a live request to download remote-control software, accept access, and pay for registration. The speaker’s later accusation that the caller was scamming him is only his characterization; it does not establish that the preceding payment-and-service pitch was merely educational content rather than a scam solicitation.

Confirm me ID and password
for the registration, you have to pay 25 euros
You tried to you tried to scam me

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted actions are the caller’s conduct within a documented investigation, not an offer made by the video creator to viewers. The payment is requested by the alleged caller, while the recording’s stated purpose was to determine whether that caller was genuine. Nothing in these quotations shows that viewers are asked to pay, download software, or obtain a reward from the video itself.

opening.argument: The combination of identity claims, escalating technical danger, remote-access instructions, and a small immediate fee is a strong scam pattern. The caller says he is acting for Microsoft, claims more than 1,000 junk and hacking files are present, and warns the computer may crash. He then directs the user toward Supremo and an external connection, later declaring that the email is infected and asking for 25 euros. These are not isolated technical statements: they create fear, authority, and urgency around a paid intervention.

citations.quote: I'm calling you from windows operating systems on behalf of Microsoft Corporation
right now more than 1,000 junk files and hacking files are present in your computer
Suprimo Control .com and just click it okay?
Your email address is also infected by detecting spy
for the registration, you have to pay 25 euros

rebuttal.rebuttal: The investigation framing does not negate the red flags visible in the actual exchange. The authority claim, alarming infection narrative, remote-control setup, and payment demand all appear in sequence. Describing the call as recorded evidence may explain why it was captured, but it does not make the underlying conduct non-scam-like or eliminate the deceptive pressure directed at the person on the call.

citations.quote: your computer can be crashed down in any point of time due to this infection
we can connect you to the rescue team of Microsoft Corporation
even your email address is not safe
you have to pay 25 euros

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These red flags are evidence about the caller being investigated, not evidence that the video itself solicits a payment or promotes remote access. The description explicitly says the recording was made after prior scam calls and warns viewers not to permit unknown computer checks. The alarming claims are presented as material to expose, not as claims viewers are asked to accept.

citations.quote: After I have been called by scammers for the second time, I used my daughter's camera setup to record this.
Never let an unknown check from your computer!
You tried to you tried to scam me, so I'm wasting your time.

opening.argument: Although the surrounding presentation can be read as a warning, the substantive material functions as a scam demonstration with a complete participation pathway. It supplies the caller’s alleged Microsoft identity, the technical scare story, the exact remote-access sequence, the connection step, and the paid registration demand. The title itself foregrounds “Scammers” and “Microsoft Tech Support,” while the exchange culminates in a 25-euro request for protection and repair. A warning label does not change the fact that the dominant content is an actionable scam pitch.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The claimed warning role is not enough to overcome how much of the material is devoted to the pitch itself. Viewers hear the authority claim, follow the remote-access route, and reach the fee request. The later accusation may be commentary, but it comes after the solicitation has already been enacted in detail, so the presentation still reproduces and centers the scam mechanism.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Reproducing a scam call for examination is not the same as promoting it. The title identifies the subject as scammers, the description says the recording was made after being called by scammers, and the speaker says he wanted to test whether the caller was genuine. The pitch is therefore the object of scrutiny; the quoted material does not show viewer-directed promotion by the video.
